https://www.romania-insider.com/romania-.text: Energy Romania’s nuclear reactor to remain in operation at least a week 05 August 2026 Iulian Ernst Like this article? Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romania’s Nuclearelectrica announced that after the detonation of a rock obstructing the flow of water on the Danube by the Naval Forces on August 3, the water level at Cernavoda nuclear power plant increased by 2 cm, reversing the downward trend. As a result of the works on the Danube, the nuclear reactor still in operation can operate for at least a week – instead of five days estimated previously, according to Cernavoda NPP manager Romeo Urjan cited by B1 TV on August 4. The planned sinking of ships loaded with rocks on one of the Danube’s arms with the aim of increasing the flow on the arm delivering water to Cernavoda NPP was not yet carried out, and this operation is expected to further extend the operation period for the nuclear reactor. Cernavoda NPP keeps in operation one of its two 680 MW reactors, which allows the country to overcome the 7,000-7,500 MW consumption peak during the 20:00-23-00 period while at the same time delivering electricity to Moldova that critically relies on electricity imports. Some one-third of Romania’s own consumption (namely nearly 2,500 MW of 7,000-7,500 MW) was covered by imports during the peak consumption period last night, according to Digi24, while the country was exporting roughly one-tenth of its output to Moldova (meaning some 500 MW). The situation remains fragile, however. Hydrological data indicate a very low flow of the Danube, and authorities have previously warned that Unit 2 could be shut down preemptively if the water level falls below technical thresholds. Such a shutdown would not pose a safety risk to the plant, but would remove significant production capacity from the system. Separately, the government of Romania is preparing to institute a mechanism for disconnecting from the power grid large industrial consumers as a means to address possible power shortages. The targeted companies would be notified 24 hours in advance, interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan announced on August 4. The initiative is presented as a measure of last resort and would be introduced by a government decision. The announcement refers to large industrial consumers, not household consumers. Previously, PM Bolojan had explained that the mechanism would be implemented through the National Energy Dispatcher within Transelectrica. The consumption allowed to each company would be established depending on the technology used and the energy available in the system at the respective times. The government presented the measure as a safety solution, which would be activated only if the voluntary reduction does not yield results. iulian@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Nuclearelectrica) Read next 04 August 2026 Energy Romania hopes to delay nuclear plant shutdown after diverting Danube waters Normal Energy Romania’s nuclear reactor to remain in operation at least a week 05 August 2026 Iulian Ernst Like this article? Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP View image in fullscreen First home buyers feel the sentiment has turned in their favour while investors feel it has swung against them, a property expert says. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP Housing ‘Pent-up demand’: First home buyers chase more loans as property investors step back, data shows Exclusive: New entrants the only cohort making more loan applications amid interest rate rises and tax changes, mortgage broker says Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google First home buyers are still taking out a large number of loans, with government backing, even as investors step back from Australia’s property market. New entrants are now the only cohort applying for more loans than they were in June, according to new data from Loan Market, the mortgage broking company. Home buying had slowed after interest rates rose three times and Labor abolished negative gearing for most investment purchases. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has said the reform was meant to “level the playing field” for first home buyers. Loan Market reported first-timer applications dropped 3% in July then rose 10% into the first half of August on a weekly average basis. Applications from other owner-occupiers and investors were roughly steady in August compared to June. Home loan demand had been falling across the board by June, down 5.4% compared to the prior quarter, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. While the number of investor loans fell by 8.6%, the number of first-time buyer mortgages fell only 2.9% on a seasonally adjusted basis, the ABS reported. First home purchases were still higher in NSW and the Australian Capital Territory than the same time the year before. They rose to hit their highest level since 2021 in South Australia and Tasmania. Could you save money on your mortgage? As house prices cool and lender rivalry heats up, experts say Australians should ask Read more Peter Esho, the chief executive of property finance firm 13x, said new entrants to the market had become more visible in recent months. “First home buyers, I think, now feel like the sentiment has swung in their favour, and investors feel like the sentiment swung against them,” Esho said. “There’s been a lot of buyers on the sideline for a long time … so that pent-up demand is going to keep it for the next few years and policy is obviously a big driver.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Esho said demand was concentrating on properties with prices close to the eligibility caps set by the government’s 5% deposit scheme. The program allows first-time buyers to borrow up to 95% of a property’s value and have the government guarantee the loan, waiving costly lenders’ mortgage insurance (LMI). Prices have fallen across Australia but properties eligible for the guarantee have seen slower price falls than homes outside the scheme, according to data company Cotality. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Property price change graph Homes are eligible if they are below $1.5m in New South Wales cities, $1m for south-east Queensland, $950,000 for Melbourne and Geelong, $850,000 for Perth, $900,000 for Adelaide and $700,000 for Hobart. Labor expanded the scheme and scrapped income caps for applicants in October 2025. Housing Australia, which administers the scheme, found applicants typically saved more than $15,000 in LMI for the median deposit paid on the median home purchased under the 5% deposit scheme. More than 320,000 people have become homeowners under the scheme since it was established in 2020. The housing minister, Clare O’Neil, told Guardian Australia that scheme participants had collectively saved more than $2.5bn in LMI by the end of July. “We know that for too long the housing market has been stacked against young people and without this scheme many wouldn’t be able to enter the market at all,” O’Neil said. More than 5,000 new guarantees had been issued each month since February. Housing Australia said that slipped just below 5,000 in July, which was still more than had been issued in any month before Labor expanded the scheme. Australia’s leading LMI company, Helia, has estimated the scheme’s expansion cost it nearly $9m worth of first home buyer business in the first half of 2026. Its remaining customers were typically people buying above the price caps or from non-participating banks, a spokesperson said. ANZ, which began offering the 5% scheme in March, was the only big four bank to maintain a steady value of mortgage applications in the June quarter. The influx of first home buyers offset a drop in lending to other groups. Scheme participants now account for one in every 20 new loan applications at ANZ. (WNDU) - A confusing decision awaits some Kosciusko County voters when they head to the polls this November. Due to an Indiana election deadline, voters will see an unexpected choice in a Warsaw school board race, despite one of the candidates officially bowing out. Some local ballots will display two names running for the Warsaw Community Schools District 7 seat. On that list is Ben Rice. However, Rice says he is no longer actively campaigning for the spot. “I realized that I wouldn’t be the school board member that District 7 deserves,” Rice said. Rice said he ended his campaign this week after a lot of consideration. Now he is throwing his support behind his opponent, Ryan Parker. “I’m very comfortable that anyone voting for me, or anyone close to me, vote for Ryan Parker,” Rice said. Even though Rice does not plan to continue his campaign, election officials cannot simply take his name off the ballot. Under Indiana law, the deadline for school board candidates to voluntarily withdraw was July 15 at noon. “I just want to be very clear with the public that I will not be serving in this capacity, even though I will still be on the ballot,” Rice explained. Because his name remains on the ballot, it is possible Rice could still receive enough votes to win the election. Local voters say the situation is bound to cause issues on Election Day. “That’s confusing and misleading,” voter Molly Alexander said. “A lot of people do not pay attention to things. There are going to be votes going to someone that’s not running when it should be going to the actual candidate.” If Rice does win and decides not to take office, the District 7 seat will be left vacant. While election officials acknowledge the next steps would be unusual, they said they are prepared to navigate the legal protocols to fill the vacancy if it happens. For now, both names will stay on the ballot, and voters will have the final say when they head to the polls this November. Stay up to date on local news with WNDU on-air and online. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rr.text: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday By Rachel Clun Business reporter ,Â Reporting from New York Published 13 November 2026 Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world. Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover. The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide. Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents. Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers. Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday. By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America. Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost? Published 9 hours ago Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world Published 10 hours ago In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected , as were some schools and police forces. UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network. In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails. In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook. Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday. In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook. The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals. Image source, Peter Pentz Image caption, Pete says his business has been brought to a standstill Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business was basically brought to a "standstill". His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" was been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations". Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she was due to complete her first house purchase today after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that. "The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies. "We're not the only one completing today, there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible," Georgia said. 'Encouraging recovery signals' Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally. While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world. By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region. Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously." Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered. A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review. Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services. "The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure. Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem. "Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said . "In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."
